sessions.title: The Cost of the Open Door
sessions.aim: To bring hospitality home to the people the reader actually meets, the lonely, the immigrant and the outsider, and to name the real cost of an open door without making it sentimental, setting aside both the fear that keeps the door locked and the cheap welcome that costs nothing.
sessions.summary:
It's one thing to admire Abraham and another to answer your own door. This last session brings hospitality down to the street you live on, where the stranger isn't a traveler in a robe but the widow across the hall, the immigrant family no one will hire, the coworker nobody sits with. The question is no longer what hospitality means but what it costs, because Scripture never pretends an open door is free.

The case for limits is wise. No one can meet every need, compassion without limits ends in the collapse of the person giving it, and guilt-driven welcome is its own kind of foolishness. This study honors limits. But the language of boundaries can quickly become the permanent reason the door stays shut against everyone. And Scripture isn't vague about the stranger our moment most wants to turn away: "Love the sojourner, therefore, for you were sojourners in the land of Egypt" (Deuteronomy 10:19). The policy questions are hard, and this isn't legal or political advice, but the command to love the actual sojourner in front of you is plain.

Every real welcome costs the host something. We were welcomed at infinite cost, by a Savior who gave his own body. The open door is expensive because grace was. The study ends with a threshold and a decision.

keyScripture.why: "For I was hungry and you gave me food, I was thirsty and you gave me drink, I was a stranger and you welcomed me" (Matthew 25:35). Jesus puts the welcome of the outsider at the center of the last judgment and identifies himself with the stranger at the door.

discussion.q: Who is the actual stranger in your life right now: someone lonely, foreign to your world, or inconvenient, whom you already know?
discussion.behind: Make it concrete. Up to now the study could stay safely in the Bible. This is where it lands on a real person each member already knows and maybe avoids. Gently push past "people like that" to one person. Nobody has to say a name aloud.

discussion.q: What's true about the need for boundaries? Has "boundaries" ever become a way of saying no to everyone?
discussion.behind: Hold both halves. Limits are wise and burnout helps no one, and the study honors them. But "boundaries" is also one of the most fluent excuses of our time, a word that can make a shut door sound healthy. Help the room tell a real limit from a fear that has learned the vocabulary of self-care.

discussion.q: Read Leviticus 19:33-34 and Deuteronomy 10:18-19. Why do you think commands about the sojourner are among the easiest for churches to explain away?
discussion.behind: Keep this pastoral, not partisan, and don't flinch either. The commands about the sojourner are unusually clear and often ignored, and the reasons are frequently political rather than biblical, on every side. The point isn't to score for a party. It's to notice how readily the fears of our culture can overwrite a clear and repeated command. Start with yourself, not with the other side.

discussion.q: What has hospitality actually cost you? What cost have you been unwilling to pay?
discussion.behind: This is the center of the session. A welcome that risks and spends nothing is a counterfeit, and the real thing has a price: time, comfort, some safety, a tidy life. Let people name both what they've paid and what they've refused, and answer first yourself.

discussion.q: Read Romans 15:7. How does what you might pay to welcome someone look next to what it cost Christ to welcome you?
discussion.behind: End in the gospel and let the weight stand. The point isn't to shame the room into trying harder. It's to see our costs as an echo of grace. Don't wrap it up with a plan. Let the threshold and the decision be the last thing in the room.

objections.objection: You have to have boundaries. No one can help everyone, and people who try to meet every need burn out, neglect their own families and end up useless to anybody. Endless open-door hospitality is a recipe for exhaustion and resentment.
objections.response: That's true, and this study means it. Limits are real and wise. No one can meet every need, and a person who tries to save everyone often wrecks their own household in the attempt. Peter's "without grumbling" (1 Peter 4:9) already warns against a welcome that sours into resentment. But "boundaries" can easily become a word laid over a door that was already shut, the language of self-care covering a self-protection that was never going to open. A real limit says, I can welcome this person and not that one this month. A false one says, I have boundaries, and welcomes no one, ever. The test is simple and uncomfortable. If your boundaries have never once been crossed by an actual costly welcome, they aren't protecting a generous life. They're walls around a closed one.

objections.objection: Immigration is a complicated political and legal issue. You can't quote "love the sojourner" as though it settles questions of borders, law and national policy. Using Scripture that way is naive and ignores real concerns about security and fairness.
objections.response: The complexity is real, and this study doesn't pretend otherwise. Questions of law, borders and national policy are hard. They involve competing goods and real concerns about security and fairness, faithful Christians disagree about them, and Scripture doesn't hand anyone a finished immigration policy. Nothing here is legal or political advice. But notice the move the objection is tempted to make: from "the policy is complicated," which is true, to "the command doesn't apply to me," which doesn't follow. Whatever a nation's laws should be, each believer still meets actual sojourners, a real family, a real neighbor, a real face. About that person Scripture isn't vague at all: "You shall love him as yourself" (Leviticus 19:34). The complexity of policy is real, and it can also become a respectable fog we hide in to avoid a command that was always about the person in front of us.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: Is there a stranger you've decided not to welcome? What cost were you unwilling to pay, and is the reason a real limit or a locked door?
sessions.practice: This week, take the one person this session brought to mind, someone lonely, foreign to your world, or simply outside, and pay one real cost to welcome them: an afternoon, a meal, an inconvenience that actually costs you something. Don't try to solve their whole life. Cross one threshold. Tell God what cost you've been refusing, and ask whether it's a limit or a wall. Write down who it was, what it cost, and what you found on the other side of the door.
sessions.closingPrayer: Lord, you were the stranger, and you told us that when we welcomed the least of these we welcomed you. We've admired Abraham and locked our own doors. We've used the language of boundaries to bless a coldness we never meant to warm, and the language of complexity to excuse ourselves from a command that was always simple and personal. Forgive us for the strangers we've chosen not to see. You welcomed us at infinite cost, giving your own body while we were still far off. Give us an open door and a willingness to pay what welcome costs, because grace was never cheap, and neither is the love that answers it. Amen.
reflection: Who is the particular person, lonely or foreign or inconvenient, whom I already know and have quietly decided not to welcome?
Where has the language of boundaries become a wall in my life?
What has my welcome actually cost me, what cost am I refusing, and how does it look beside what God paid to welcome me?
sessions.teaching:
It's one thing to admire Abraham running in the heat, and quite another to answer your own door. So this last session takes hospitality down out of the tents and upper rooms of Scripture and sets it on the street where you live, because that's where the whole study was always heading, and it's where it's easiest to avoid.

In your life, the stranger isn't a picturesque traveler with a staff. The stranger is the widow across the hall who hasn't had a visitor in weeks and whose television you can hear through the wall. It's the immigrant family down the block the neighborhood has quietly decided not to see, whose English is halting and whose need is real. It's the coworker nobody eats lunch with, the new family at church that nobody has invited home, the person whose presence is inconvenient and whose loneliness is a fact. And once the stranger has a face, the question changes. It's no longer what hospitality means, which we could discuss all day without moving. It's what hospitality costs, because Scripture never pretends the open door is free.

The case for boundaries deserves to be heard first, because it's wise, and I won't caricature it as selfishness. No one can meet every need. A person who tries to save everyone ends up saving no one, neglecting their own family and running themselves into the ground. Compassion with no limits doesn't grow into sainthood. It collapses. Peter himself guarded against the welcome that turns to resentment when he wrote "without grumbling" (1 Peter 4:9). Limits aren't the enemy of love. Sometimes they're its discipline.

But watch how quickly the wise thing becomes the excuse. "Boundaries" may be the most fluent word in our vocabulary, and it will bless almost anything. It can name a real limit that protects a generous life, and it can just as easily lay a coat of therapeutic language over a door that was already shut, and from the outside the two sound exactly alike. The test is uncomfortable and simple. If your boundaries have never once been crossed by an actual costly welcome, if they've only ever kept people out and never been spent on anyone, then they aren't protecting a generous life. They're walls around a closed one.

Then there's the stranger our own moment most wants to turn away, and Scripture isn't vague about him. Again and again the law and the prophets return to the sojourner, the foreigner living among God's people. "You shall not wrong a sojourner or oppress him, for you were sojourners in the land of Egypt" (Exodus 22:21). "When a stranger sojourns with you in your land, you shall not do him wrong. You shall treat the stranger who sojourns with you as the native among you, and you shall love him as yourself" (Leviticus 19:33-34). God himself "loves the sojourner, giving him food and clothing. Love the sojourner, therefore, for you were sojourners in the land of Egypt" (Deuteronomy 10:18-19). This isn't a modern question Scripture happens to be silent on. The sojourner is a named and repeated object of God's particular care.

The policy questions are hard, and I don't want to pretend they aren't. Law, borders and the common good are real and complicated, Christians who take the Bible seriously disagree about them, and nothing here is a tidy answer to any of it, or legal advice, or a party's talking point. But notice the move all of us are tempted to make, from "the policy is complicated," which is true, straight to "the command doesn't touch me," which doesn't follow. Whatever the law should be, you still meet actual sojourners, a real family with real faces, and about them Scripture couldn't be clearer. I've hidden in the complexity of an issue to avoid the simplicity of a person. I've called a locked door a boundary. I've admired the strangers in the Bible and passed by the ones on my own street.

So the study ends, not with a technique or a program, but with the cost. Every real welcome costs the host something: time you wanted for yourself, comfort you'd rather keep, safety you can't fully guarantee, the tidy and defended life you've built. A welcome that costs nothing was never what Scripture meant by the word. And the reason we know it is that we were welcomed at infinite cost. God didn't open his door cheaply. Christ gave his own body and blood, and welcomed us while we were still strangers and enemies and far off. "Welcome one another as Christ has welcomed you, for the glory of God" (Romans 15:7). On the last day he will say, "I was a stranger and you welcomed me" (Matthew 25:35), or he will say that we didn't. The open door is expensive because grace was expensive. There's a threshold in front of you and a stranger on the other side of it, and no one can make that decision for you.

scriptureStudy.note: "I was a stranger and you welcomed me." And, "as you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me." Christ identifies himself with the stranger so fully that welcoming the outsider is welcoming him, and turning the outsider away is turning him away.

God "loves the sojourner, giving him food and clothing. Love the sojourner, therefore, for you were sojourners in the land of Egypt." God's own care for the foreigner is the ground and pattern of Israel's, and the memory of having been strangers drives the command.

"You shall love him as yourself, for you were strangers in the land of Egypt." The command to love your neighbor as yourself (Leviticus 19:18) is extended in the same chapter to the foreigner, closing the loophole that would keep love inside the tribe.

"The sojourner has not lodged in the street; I have opened my doors to the traveler." Job offers his open door as evidence of a righteous life. Welcoming the stranger isn't an extra. It's a basic mark of integrity before God.

"Is not this the fast that I choose" asks God, and he answers with bread for the hungry and "the homeless poor" brought "into your house." He rejects a piety that won't open its home and names the welcome of the destitute as the worship he wants.

A Samaritan, the despised outsider, stops for the beaten man, "had compassion," bandages his wounds, takes him to an inn and pays for his care. He becomes the picture of costly welcome, spending real money and real time on a stranger while the respectable pass by on the other side.

"Therefore welcome one another as Christ has welcomed you, for the glory of God." Paul grounds every human welcome in the divine one, so our open door echoes Christ's and is measured against what his welcome cost.

sessions.goingDeeper:
For a group that wants more, press on the two hard edges of this session: the cost of welcome, and the stranger who is an immigrant. Both are places where the church's practice most often fails and most often explains itself away. On cost, take up Christine Pohl's argument in Making Room that Christian hospitality has always carried cost and some risk, welcoming strangers without a guarantee of safety or reward, and that our insistence on a fully controlled, risk-free welcome may be part of what has hollowed the practice out. Weigh, carefully and without recklessness, the difference between prudence and the kind of total risk-aversion that makes real hospitality nearly impossible.

On the sojourner, look at how much the Old Testament says. The Hebrew word ger, the resident foreigner, appears dozens of times in the law alone. Set that beside the church's frequent silence, and ask whether our politics, whichever way they run, have shaped our reading of Scripture more than Scripture has shaped our politics. Hold two things together here. Immigration policy is a contested, second-order question on which faithful Christians land in different places, and this study doesn't settle it. The command to love the actual sojourner you meet isn't contested.

Finally, look ahead. Jesus said that "many will come from east and west and recline at table with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven" (Matthew 8:11). Every open door now is a small rehearsal of that feast, and every door closed for good is a quiet denial of it. Send the group out with that picture: the stranger at the door, and the Christ who was himself a stranger.
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose a couple in your group have welcomed people for years, and they're tired. With real weariness rather than excuse-making, they say they've given and given and been taken advantage of, and they've learned they need boundaries now. They aren't cold. They have scars from actually opening the door.

Honor the scars before you press anything. They aren't the closed-door people this session warns about. They've paid real costs, their weariness is earned and their need for limits is legitimate. Say so plainly and mean it, because lecturing people who are spent about generosity is its own cruelty.

Then, gently, help them see the difference between the limits of a generous life that needs to recover and limits that quietly close the door for good. A wise limit says, not now, or not this one, or not alone. A wall says, never again, and turns the wound into a policy. Protect their need for rest, and when they're ready, ask whether the door is closing to heal or closing to stay closed. Ask the group how they might share the load so that no one's door has to carry it all.

memoryVerse.text: As you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me.

leaderPrimer:
The particular danger of a hospitality study is that it's the easiest study in the world to enjoy and never obey. It's warm and pleasant, and a group can spend five weeks admiring Abraham and the early church and Jesus among the sinners and go home without opening a single door. Admiration is the counterfeit of obedience, and it's especially tempting here because the subject is so pleasant to talk about. So set the rule the first night and keep it: this study isn't finished when we understand hospitality. It's finished when someone in the room has actually welcomed a stranger. Keep pulling the conversation away from the stranger in general and toward the particular person each member already knows, the lonely or foreign or inconvenient one they already avoid. That person is the point.

Watch for two opposite reactions. The first is the showroom instinct: people who can't imagine welcoming anyone because their home isn't nice enough or their life isn't tidy enough. They need to hear, more than once, that hospitality isn't entertaining, that a plain table in a plain room is exactly what Scripture means, and that introverts, the poor and the overwhelmed are as much called to this as anyone. The second is the fortress instinct: people who have quietly decided their home is a private retreat the world doesn't enter. They'll need the gentle, steady pressure of what Scripture actually says.

Handle the fifth session with particular care. It names the immigrant and the outsider plainly, and some of that will touch people's politics. Keep it pastoral and personal rather than partisan. Name the evasion in yourself before anyone else's, grant that immigration policy is hard and that faithful Christians disagree about it, and don't let the complexity of policy become a fog that hides the simplicity of the person in front of us.

Lead from inside the study, not above it. If you present yourself as the expert host, the group will admire you and change nothing. Go in as someone still learning to open a door that keeps wanting to stay shut. Five weeks won't turn a group into the early church. They can turn admiration into a first open door, and send a few people home to set one more place for someone who can't pay them back.

faq.q: Is this study going to make people feel guilty for not having a nice enough home to host?
faq.a: No. Freeing people from that is the aim of the first session. The study takes on the modern habit of turning hospitality into entertaining, a performance in a presentable home for guests who are expected to return the favor. Scripture's word isn't the dinner party. It's philoxenia, love of the stranger, and it assumes a plain table in a plain room. The pressure to impress has stopped more welcome than selfishness has, because people who can't host beautifully often decide not to host at all. The study says plainly that introverts, the poor and the overwhelmed are called and able to do this as much as anyone, and that a stranger needs a chair, not a showroom. Nobody should finish feeling their home isn't good enough.

faq.q: What's the difference between hospitality and entertaining, and why does the study make so much of it?
faq.a: Entertaining is a gathering of friends in a presentable home, and it runs quietly on reciprocity, a ledger of invitations given and expected back. Hospitality, in the word Scripture uses, is love of the xenos, the stranger, the one who can't repay you. Jesus drew the line himself when he told a host not to invite friends and rich neighbors who would invite him back, but the poor who couldn't (Luke 14:12-14). The study makes much of it because the swap is nearly invisible and it changes what we think God is asking. Entertaining is a good thing, and the feast of friends is a real gift. But it isn't the same as the command, and a circle that only ever seats people who can seat us back is smaller than what Scripture means.

faq.q: Does the study say it's wrong to have friends over for dinner?
faq.a: No, and it says so plainly. Gathering friends around a table is one of the good gifts of this life, a foretaste of the wedding feast. The study doesn't ask anyone to stop enjoying their friends or to turn every meal into a mission. What it presses on is the meal that is only ever with friends, the circle that never opens to someone who can't repay. Keep the feast of friends and add an empty chair for the stranger, and you have the joy of friendship and the shape of the gospel at the same table.

faq.q: Isn't it naive, even dangerous, to tell people to welcome strangers into their homes?
faq.a: The study takes the danger seriously and doesn't counsel recklessness. Wisdom is a virtue, nobody should put children or vulnerable people in harm's way, and judging a particular person in a particular situation isn't the same as having a closed heart. Abraham welcomed eagerly, not carelessly. What the study presses on is the slide from a real, specific caution into a general and permanent one, where the rare danger becomes the settled reason the door stays shut against every ordinary stranger. Prudence is real. It's also the most respectable cover a closed heart can wear, and the study asks each of us to tell the two apart. Session 2 gives this question the most time.

faq.q: Why does the study spend a whole session on who Jesus ate with?
faq.a: Because the table Jesus kept was the complaint most often made against him, and it turns out to be close to the center of the gospel. "This man receives sinners and eats with them" (Luke 15:2) was an accusation, and it's also one of the best summaries of Christianity in the Bible. In that world a shared meal declared acceptance, so when Jesus ate with tax collectors and people counted unclean, he was saying that the kingdom comes to people before they clean themselves up. He didn't lower the standard. He said the table is where the sick get well (Mark 2:17). The session asks each of us whether our own table, quietly sorted by who deserves a chair, looks more like the critics' than like Christ's.

faq.q: Does welcoming everyone mean the church has no standards and approves of everything?
faq.a: No, and the study guards against that. Jesus didn't treat sin as nothing. He called people to repentance, and a welcome that approves of everything has stopped being love. "Friend of sinners" has been used as cover by churches that lacked the nerve to say anything hard, and that betrays the Jesus they name. But the cure for a weak welcome isn't a closed one. Jesus held the open table and the hard word together, and he told the truth from inside the welcome. The order matters. Respectability says, clean up and then come to the table. Jesus says, come to the table, and this is where you'll be made clean.

faq.q: What does the study mean by calling the church a household?
faq.a: For roughly its first three centuries the church had no buildings of its own to speak of. It met in homes, ate in homes and welcomed strangers and travelers into homes, and the open door was the shape of the church rather than a program it ran. Paul lists hospitality in Romans 12 beside genuine love and blessing those who persecute you, using a verb that means to pursue it. Acts describes believers "breaking bread in their homes" with "glad and generous hearts" (Acts 2:46). The study honors what the church gained in buildings and organized care, which reach further than any one table. But it names what was lost when welcome moved entirely from the home to the agency: the stranger became a client, and no one crossed anyone's threshold.

faq.q: I'm exhausted and introverted. Is this going to guilt me into burning out?
faq.a: No. Rest is a good gift. God himself rested, and tired or introverted people aren't shut out of the kingdom. A hospitality that produces burnout and resentment has already failed Peter's "without grumbling" (1 Peter 4:9). The study sets aside the false version first, the pressure to keep a constant open house. The early Christians' homes were ordinary and tired and full of children too, and an open door never meant a door that never closed. One guest isn't a program, and once a month isn't burnout. An introvert can welcome one person well, which is often truer hospitality than a crowded room.

faq.q: How does the study handle immigration without becoming political?
faq.a: By separating two questions our culture keeps blurring. It says plainly that immigration policy is hard, that law, borders and the common good involve competing goods and real concerns, that faithful Christians disagree, and that Scripture doesn't hand anyone a finished policy. None of it is legal or political advice, and it doesn't take a party's side. But it also won't let the complexity of policy hide a command that was never about policy. Whatever a nation's laws should be, each believer still meets actual sojourners, real families and real neighbors, and about them Scripture is plain: "Love the sojourner, therefore, for you were sojourners in the land of Egypt" (Deuteronomy 10:19). The session looks for the evasion in ourselves first, not in the other side.

faq.q: Is hospitality really a command, or just a nice thing for people who enjoy it?
faq.a: It's a command, given to the whole church and not to a gifted few. Romans 12:13, Hebrews 13:2 and 1 Peter 4:9 all command it, and one of the qualifications for a church overseer is being "hospitable" (1 Timothy 3:2), which means it isn't a fringe activity. The verb in Romans 12:13 means to pursue, so it's active, not just a willingness to receive whoever happens to ask. The idea that hospitality is a personality trait for outgoing people with big houses has excused much of the church from something Scripture excuses no one from. Temperament and house size aren't the issue. The command is the same for an introvert in a small apartment as for anyone else.

faq.q: I'm a skeptic. Isn't this just religion recruiting through free meals?
faq.a: That's a fair suspicion, and the study answers it by refusing that move. The welcome it describes is given to someone who can't repay, with no agenda to fix or convert them first, because a welcome that calculates a return is exactly what Jesus attacked. If an open door is a recruiting tactic, it has already stopped being what Scripture means. What the study does make is a claim: that one of the deepest human needs is to be welcomed rather than screened. You don't have to share the faith to notice that a welcome given to people who can give nothing back is rarer than the trading of favors the world runs on, and to wonder what could make someone do it.

faq.q: How do I lead this if I'm not naturally hospitable and my own door tends to stay shut?
faq.a: That isn't a disqualification. The study was written to be led by ordinary people, not gifted hosts, and every question carries notes for the leader. What you need isn't a naturally open home, which few people have. It's a willingness to go first: to name your own closed door and your own habit of screening people, and to keep the room safe for people who feel they're failing at this. If you present yourself as the expert, the group will admire you and change nothing. Your own struggle to open the door, named plainly, lets you stand alongside everyone else. Read the leader's notes, name your own locked door, and go first.

timeline.event: Abraham runs from his tent in the heat of the day to welcome three strangers and sets a feast before men he doesn't know, who turn out to be the Lord and two angels (Genesis 18). It becomes the founding story of biblical hospitality.

The law given at Sinai binds Israel again and again to the sojourner: the stranger is to be treated as the native and loved as oneself, because Israel too was once a stranger in Egypt (Leviticus 19, Deuteronomy 10).
The prophecy in Isaiah 58 names the fast God actually wants: not private piety but an open house, sharing bread with the hungry and bringing the homeless poor inside.
Jesus keeps a table so scandalous that he's called a friend of tax collectors and sinners, eats with people before they change, and teaches that welcoming the stranger is welcoming him (Matthew 25).
The early church in Acts eats in homes day by day and holds its goods loosely. In the mid-50s Paul tells the Romans to pursue hospitality (Romans 12:13).

timeline.date: Late first to early second century
timeline.event: Traveling teachers and believers on the move depend on the open homes of Christians. The Didache and the letters of John give instructions for receiving them, and 3 John calls such support partnership in the truth.
Basil of Caesarea founds a great complex for the poor, the sick and travelers on the edge of his city, later called the Basileias, carrying Christian hospitality into organized care on a new scale.
The Rule of Benedict tells monks to receive every guest as Christ (chapter 53), building the welcome of strangers, including the washing of guests' feet, into the daily life of the monastery.
Monasteries, hospitals and hostels across Christian Europe care for travelers and the sick. The words hospital, hostel and hospice all come from the Latin hospes, which meant both guest and host.

Henri Nouwen, in Reaching Out, describes hospitality as one of the movements of the spiritual life, from hostility to hospitality: making a free space where a stranger can come in and become a friend.

Christine Pohl publishes Making Room: Recovering Hospitality as a Christian Tradition, tracing the long history of Christian welcome and what was lost when hospitality narrowed to private entertaining and impersonal service.

facilitatorScript.open: Welcome, and thanks for being here. Before we start, a word about what this study is and isn't. It isn't something we can enjoy and then go home unchanged. I'm going to keep pulling us away from welcome as a nice idea and toward real people in our real lives, so expect to be asked, more than once, who the lonely or foreign or overlooked person in your life is. It also isn't a study that shames anyone for a small home or a tired week. Hospitality isn't entertaining, and a plain table in a plain room is exactly what Scripture means. And I'm not teaching this from above it. My door tends to stay shut too. Tonight we're looking at ________. Let me read our key passage, and then we'll sit with it for a moment before anyone says anything. There are no wrong answers in the first five minutes.
facilitatorScript.transition: We've looked hard at what this passage says. Now let's bring it home, off the page and onto the street each of us lives on, to a real person we could welcome or could avoid, because none of this matters if the stranger stays an idea.
facilitatorScript.close: Let's stop there. I'm not going to tie this off with a neat plan, because hospitality isn't something you solve in an evening. Take the weight of it home with you. Try the practice this week, in your own home, with a real person, even if it's awkward. Spend some time with the reflection questions. And come back ready to tell the truth about how it went, even if it didn't go well. The test of this study isn't whether we understood it. It's whether a door opened. Let me pray for us before we go.

plan: Week 1: Orientation. Read the summary together, set the rule that admiration is not obedience, and walk session 1's opening questions slowly.
Week 2: Session 1, Philoxenia, Not the Dinner Party, full discussion and practice.
Week 3: Session 2, Abraham, the Three Strangers, and Angels Unaware, with extended time on prudence and the closed door.
Week 4: Session 3, The Table Jesus Kept, part one, sitting with the scandal of who he ate with.
Week 5: Session 3 continued, the standards objection handled carefully and the practice of the uncomfortable guest list.
Week 6: Session 4, The Church as Household, on the home church and the privatized home.
Week 7: Session 5, The Cost of the Open Door, with the immigrant and the outsider named plainly and pastorally.
Week 8: Integration. Revisit all five practices, the scripture index, and the actual doors each member has opened or intends to, closing in the welcome of Christ.

glossary.definition: The Greek word the New Testament uses for hospitality, built from phileo, to love, and xenos, the stranger. It means love of the stranger, not love of the guest list you already have, and it's the word used in Romans 12:13 and Hebrews 13:2, with its related adjective in 1 Peter 4:9.
The Greek word for stranger, foreigner or guest: the person who isn't yet a friend and can't repay you. The one the love in philoxenia is for.

The modern stand-in for hospitality: a gathering in a presentable home for guests who can return the favor, running quietly on reciprocity. The feast of friends is a real good, but it isn't the command and shouldn't be confused with welcoming the stranger.

In Hebrew, the ger: the resident foreigner, someone living among God's people who wasn't born one of them. The law names the sojourner dozens of times as an object of God's particular care, and Israel is told to love the sojourner because Israel had been a sojourner in Egypt.

The phrase from Hebrews 13:2, which looks back to Abraham at Mamre. It doesn't promise that every stranger is secretly wonderful. It reminds us that we can't see in advance what a welcome will become, which takes away our excuse for turning an ordinary stranger away.

The quiet exchange Jesus challenged in Luke 14: the invitation given in expectation of being repaid. It's the instinct that closes the circle of the table, and grace breaks it by welcoming someone who can't pay anything back.

A phrase some scholars use for Jesus's habit of eating across the social boundaries of his culture, sharing tables with tax collectors, sinners and people counted unclean. It was a parable acted out at the table: the God he proclaimed doesn't sort his guests the way society sorts its tables.

Paul's phrase for the church (1 Timothy 3:15; see also Ephesians 2:19). For its first centuries the church was a household in a literal sense too, meeting, eating and welcoming strangers mostly in homes.

This study's name for the modern home treated as a defended retreat, a place to shut the world out. The early church wouldn't have recognized it. It's more than a lifestyle preference. It says something about the heart.
The false measure that turns hospitality into an impressive home and a flawless meal. It stops more welcome than selfishness does, because people who can't host beautifully decide not to host at all.

The image at the center of Pohl's book and close to Nouwen's: clearing a space, in your home and in yourself, for a stranger to enter. Introverts and poor families can do it as well as anyone, because it isn't about impressive hosting.

The truth this study won't make sentimental: every real welcome costs the host something, whether time, comfort, some safety or a tidy life. A welcome that costs nothing was never what Scripture meant, and the welcome we received cost Christ everything.

A wise limit that protects a generous life, and also one of the most fluent excuses of our time, self-care language laid over a door that was already shut. The study asks us to tell a real limit from a wall that only calls itself one.

promoKit.bulletinBlurb: Hospitality usually gets taught as a nicer dinner party, and almost nobody stops to ask what the word means. This five-session study goes past entertaining to what Scripture actually commands: philoxenia, love of the stranger, a welcome for people who can't repay you. It looks at Abraham running to meet three strangers in the heat, the table Jesus kept and the scandal of who he ate with, the early church as a household with an open door, and the real cost of welcoming the lonely, the immigrant and the outsider today. It's plain about the cost and freeing about the plain table. Anyone can lead it with no preparation.
promoKit.pulpitAnnouncement: We're starting a five-week study on hospitality, and before anyone pictures a cooking class, let me say what it isn't. It isn't about entertaining, and it isn't about having a nice enough home. It's about the word Scripture uses, love of the stranger, and it moves from Abraham and the three visitors to the table Jesus kept to the lonely and the immigrant on our own streets. It deals plainly with the hard parts, including what an open door costs. I'll be learning it right alongside you, because my own door tends to stay shut. There's no homework, and no preparation needed to lead a group. Sign up at the welcome table.

quoteCards: Scripture has no word for the dinner party. It has a word for love of the stranger.
Abraham ran before he knew who they were. The welcome comes before the recognition, or it doesn't come at all.
"This man receives sinners and eats with them." They meant it as an accusation. It's the gospel.
Jesus didn't lower the standard. He moved the place of healing. The table is where the sick get well.
For its first centuries the church met in homes. The door was the point.
We made the home a fortress and handed the welcome to professionals, and called both progress.
A welcome that costs the host nothing was never what Scripture meant.
The open door is expensive because grace was expensive.
